query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of aluminum (e.g., ~3–5 atomic percent) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will enable the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 surface scale during high-temperature exposure in air, thereby improving oxygen resistance while preserving its good room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small alloying addition of aluminum (approximately 3–5 at.%) into the melt stream during casting.
generation.conditions: High-temperature air exposure at around 800 °C for a duration up to 5 hours; mechanical performance evaluations at room temperature (tensile ductility) and at high temperature (yield strength at 1000 °C, strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, continuous Al2O3 scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the added aluminum preferentially oxidizes to form a stable, slow-growing, adherent Al2O3 layer that acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress. This protective oxide minimizes internal oxidation (pesting) without adversely affecting the inherent solid‐solution strengthening and ductility of the HfNbTaTiZr matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the Al-doped alloy will exhibit a significantly reduced oxidation rate (as evidenced by lower mass gain and less oxide penetration) during high-temperature air exposure while maintaining comparable room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which, although mechanically promising at both room and high temperatures, shows rapid oxidation (pesting) when exposed to air at ~800 °C.
generation.boundary: Temperature of approximately 800 °C in an air atmosphere over an exposure duration of up to 5 hours; mechanical property assessments must be performed under conditions similar to prior studies (i.e., room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield tests at 1000 °C with a strain rate range of 10−4–10−2 s−1).
generation.uncertainty: While the Al2O3 scale is expected to improve oxygen resistance, the precise Al concentration required to balance the oxide protection with retention of desirable mechanical properties needs optimization. There is uncertainty regarding potential phase changes or brittle intermetallic formation at higher Al additions, which must be evaluated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of samples: one using the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy and the other with an additional 3–5 at.% Al. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Characterize the surface oxide layers using XRD and SEM/EDS to confirm the presence and continuity of the Al2O3 scale on the Al-doped alloy. Measure the oxidation weight gain and compare the mechanical properties (room-temperature tensile ductility and 1000 °C yield strength) of both sets.
measurements: Phase identification and morphology of surface oxide scales (e.g., via XRD and SEM/EDS)
High-temperature yield strength at 1000 °C (strain rate 10−4–10−2 s−1)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped samples do not form a protective, continuous Al2O3 scale, exhibit similar or greater oxidation (i.e., similar mass gain or oxide penetration) compared to the undoped alloy, or show significant degradation in mechanical properties (ductility or yield strength), then the hypothesis is falsified.
